title: Sarah's burial (Genesis 23)
hook: Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah and pays in full to bury his wife with dignity

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Akedah, the binding of Isaac. Your line was the tradition wrestles here. Did you let one hard question stay open? Day forty-nine.

Sarah dies at a hundred and twenty-seven, in Hebron. The woman who left everything with Abraham, who laughed behind the tent flap, who held her impossible son. In the old JPS translation: "and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her." And then Abraham has a very practical problem, the one everyone who has lost someone knows. There's a body, and there's nowhere to put it. He's lived in this land for decades. God promised all of it to him and his children. And he doesn't own a single square foot. So he gets up from beside his dead wife and goes to talk to the local people, the children of Heth, about buying a grave.
screen: `A HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SEVEN.` → `TO MOURN AND TO WEEP.` → `NOWHERE TO BURY HER.`

segments.voice: Abraham introduces himself with a line that sounds like every immigrant who ever stood in a government office: "I am a stranger and a sojourner with you." Sell me a burial place. The locals answer politely: you're a mighty prince among us, bury her in the best of our graves. But Abraham wants one place: the cave of Machpelah, at the edge of a field belonging to a man named Ephron. Ephron, in front of everyone at the city gate, says, I give it to you. Free. And Abraham says no. I'll pay for it. So Ephron names a price, casually: four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? A lot, it turns out. And Abraham weighs out the full amount, in the currency the merchants use, in front of witnesses. Why insist on paying? The commentators say: so that no one could ever say the grave wasn't his. A gift can be taken back. A purchase stands. And there's a quiet ache in it. The first piece of the promised land Abraham ever owns is a grave. Later, Abraham will be buried in that cave, and Isaac and Rebekah, and Jacob and Leah. It still stands in Hebron today. Notice, too, the order of the verse: to mourn, then to weep. The rabbis read the first as speaking about her, the eulogy, and the second as the tears. And there's a scribal detail in Torah scrolls: one letter in to weep for her is written small. Some say his tears were held in, even then. Grief deserved ground, and he paid in full.
screen: `A STRANGER AND A SOJOURNER.` · `FREE? NO. FULL PRICE.` · `THE FIRST LAND IS A GRAVE.` · `TO MOURN, THEN TO WEEP.` · then, large: `GRIEF DESERVES GROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who's gone. A grandparent, a parent, a friend, a teacher, even someone you never met but loved from a distance. Let their face come. Remember one specific thing: a phrase they said, a dish they made, the way they laughed. Stay with it. You don't have to cry, and you don't have to hold it back. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Sarah's burial. The cave of Machpelah, bought in full. And that's the seventh week: hospitality, Sarah's laugh, Sodom, Lot's wife, Hagar's well, the Akedah, and Sarah's burial.
Your line: grief deserves ground. Today, honor the memory of someone gone: light a candle, say their name aloud, tell one story about them. Day forty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition buries the dead promptly and with dignity, begins with a eulogy and mourning, and remembers them each year on the anniversary, the yahrzeit, often by lighting a candle and saying the Kaddish.

original.note: Hebrew: the cave of Machpelah, often explained as the double cave.

trapdoor: what you thought: a real-estate deal in an old story.
what it means: a grieving man, a stranger in the promised land, pays full price so his wife's grave can never be taken.
what a scholar hears: the small kaf in velivkotah (23:2) in Torah scrolls, and a midrash naming Machpelah among places bought at full price so none could dispute them.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 23:2 and 23:4.
'Mighty prince' (23:6) and Ephron's 'what is that betwixt me and thee?' (23:15) are paraphrased.
Small kaf in velivkotah: a scribal tradition (Baal HaTurim and others read it as restrained weeping). Confirm.
Genesis Rabbah 79:7: three places bought at full price (Machpelah, Joseph's tomb at Shechem, the Temple site). The trapdoor mentions only the principle. Confirm.
'To mourn, then to weep' read as eulogy then tears: a common reading (e.g. Moed Katan 27b's order of mourning). Confirm attribution.
Machpelah as 'double': Eruvin 53a gives explanations (double cave; couples). Confirm.
The cave's current site in Hebron is politically sensitive; the script says only that it still stands there. Confirm tone.
